s.h: Three common kinds of bad-faith dispute.
b: Three common kinds of bad-faith dispute.
Property & Catastrophe

First-party property losses: hail & wind, fire, winter storm, wildfire & mudslide, tornado, and civil unrest, often with business-interruption components and claim records that run to hundreds of thousands of pages.
Fair claims practices and standards of care
Whether the handling met the state’s fair claims practices statutes and regulations, the industry standard of care, and the carrier’s own written claim-handling guidelines.
Coverage and policy interpretation

Disputes that turn on what the policy says and how the carrier applied it: notice under claims-made forms, deductibles & waived conditions, the duty to defend, an agent’s representation of policy terms, and which insurer bears the extra-contractual exposure.
Conduct between insurers and policyholders.

In an insurance dispute, the only standards which govern the actions of the policyholder are the terms and conditions contained within the policy. However, an insurer’s conduct is governed by standards set forth in the policy, statutes & regulations, and industry custom & practice. Bad faith is the claim that an insurer failed to deal fairly with its own policyholder. In first-party cases, the dispute is over the policyholder’s own claim: a property, auto, life, health, or disability claim that was denied, delayed, or underpaid. In third-party cases, the insurer is accused of failing to protect its insured against a liability claim, most often by declining a settlement offer within policy limits and leaving the insured exposed to a verdict above them.

Many states also set out claim-handling duties in unfair claims settlement practices statutes and regulations, and those standards are often at the center of the dispute. Related claims arise between insurers themselves, as when an excess carrier sues the primary carrier over a failure to settle, and between policyholders and the agents who placed their coverage. Coverage questions, such as notice under claims-made policies, exclusions, deductibles, and the duty to defend, frequently run alongside the bad-faith claim.
Expert testimony in these matters usually turns on the standard of care: what a reasonable insurer would have done with the same information at the same point in the claim.
Claims against a claims professional other than the insurer, such as a third-party administrator, agency, or defense counsel, are covered under Claims Handling Review .

Preparation, presentation, and review of business interruption and property damage claims, for policyholders and insurers.
What business interruption coverage does.

Business interruption (business income) coverage replaces the income a business loses when covered physical damage forces it to suspend operations, for the period reasonably needed to restore the property. Related coverages include extra expense, extended business income after reopening, civil authority, and contingent business interruption for losses at a supplier’s or customer’s premises.

These claims are demanding to prepare and to adjust. The loss has to be measured against what the business would have earned had the damage not occurred, which means working through financial records, forecasts, the restoration timeline, and the policy’s terms. Disputes commonly involve the length of the period of restoration, the calculation of lost income, the treatment of continuing & saved expenses, and delay in payment, and they often run alongside a dispute over the property damage itself.
Business-interruption claims in litigation also appear under Property & Catastrophe .

A carrier-level review looks past the individual claim to the operation that produced it: how the claims department is staffed and supervised, what its written policies and procedures require, how reserves are set and revised, what controls exist over payments, and whether settlements are fair and consistent across the book.

These reviews are commissioned by the carrier or its counsel, by a regulator during an examination, by the receiver of a failed insurer, or by a party to litigation in which the company’s practices are at issue. They usually rest on a sample of files scored against a consistent standard, so that findings can be stated for the operation as a whole.
When an insurer fails, the same questions go to the cause of the failure: whether reserving, claim handling, and communication with claimants met regulatory and industry standards.

Built for amended Rule 702.

Amended Rule 702 of the Federal Rules of Evidence, effective December 2023, sharpened the question every expert opinion must answer: does it reflect a reliable application of reliable methods to the facts of the case?

Case-mapping is built for that question, and for its state-court analogues. The method is documented, the application is visible, and every finding traces to a Bates-numbered page or other identifiable parts of the production the court can check.

Scoring the file.

A claim audit draws a sample of files, usually at random, and scores each one against a consistent set of tests: whether coverage was confirmed, contact & investigation were timely, the reserve was set and revised properly, payments were accurate and supported, and the file documents what was done and why.

Scored this way, individual findings add up to a measure of the operation: error rates, payment accuracy, documentation quality, and compliance with the company’s guidelines and the applicable regulations. b: The standard of care for claims professionals.

Claims handling is the work of investigating, evaluating, reserving, negotiating, and paying insurance claims. Agents and brokers, and the defense counsel an insurer appoints, also shape how a claim unfolds.

s.h: Why claims and reserves are audited.
b: Why claims and reserves are audited.

A claim reserve is an insurer’s estimate of what it will ultimately pay on a claim. Reserves are frequently the largest liability on a carrier’s balance sheet and drive an insurer’s financial statements and its solvency, so regulators, auditors, reinsurers, acquirers and, when a company fails, receivers all need to know whether they are adequate.

Claim audits test how claims are actually being handled, usually by examining a random sample of files against the company’s own standards and the industry’s: whether coverage was confirmed, the investigation was timely, the reserve was set and revised properly, payments were accurate and the file was documented. Reserve adequacy studies compare held reserves with what the files support.

In an insolvency, each claim filed against the estate must also be evaluated and adjudicated before the estate can pay creditors and close. Audits and studies of this kind are typically delivered as a report or adjudication rather than as testimony, though the same analysis can later support an expert opinion.

s.h: What the policy says, and how it was applied.
b: What the policy says, and how it was applied.

Coverage disputes ask what the insurance contract promises and whether the insurer honored it. They turn on the policy language, the declarations & endorsements, the conditions the insured had to meet, and the way the insurer read and applied all of them to the facts of the claim.

Common questions include notice and reporting under claims-made policies, the reach of exclusions, deductibles, and self-insured retentions, waiver of policy conditions, the duty to defend, and what an agent told the insured about the coverage being bought. Between insurers, coverage questions decide which carrier bears a loss, including extra-contractual exposure above policy limits.

Coverage and bad faith often travel together. An insurer that misreads its own policy may also be accused of handling the claim unreasonably, and the expert’s task is to separate what the contract required from how the claim was handled.

s.h: The rules a claim is handled under.

Most states have adopted a version of the NAIC’s model Unfair Claims Settlement Practices Act. It lists practices an insurer may not engage in: misrepresenting policy provisions, failing to acknowledge and act promptly on claims, failing to adopt reasonable standards for prompt investigation, refusing to pay without a reasonable investigation, and failing to affirm or deny coverage within a reasonable time, among others. State regulations add specific deadlines and documentation requirements.

In many states these statutes do not by themselves give a policyholder a right to sue, but they are widely treated as evidence of the standard a reasonable insurer is expected to meet. Alongside them sit the industry’s customary practice and the carrier’s own claim manuals, guidelines, and training materials.

The analysis follows the claim file step by step: when the claim was reported and acknowledged, what was investigated and when, how it was evaluated, what the policyholder was told, and when and how much was paid, each measured against the standard that applied at that point in the claim.

First-party property and catastrophe claims.

First-party property claims are claims by policyholders under their own property coverage: homeowners, commercial property, and business owners policies. Catastrophe events, such as hail & windstorms, hurricanes & tornadoes, wildfire & mudslide, winter storms, and civil unrest, produce these claims in large numbers and at large values, often all at once. Mr. Bingham serves as a property insurance expert witness in these disputes, with reports written for both state and federal courts.

Disputes commonly turn on the scope and cost of the damage, whether it was caused by a covered peril, the application of exclusions & deductibles, the valuation of buildings, contents, and business personal property, the timing & amount of payments, and the business income lost while the property was being restored. When a policyholder alleges that the insurer’s handling was unreasonable, the dispute becomes a bad-faith claim as well as a contract claim.

When the parties agree that a loss is covered but disagree on its amount, the policy’s appraisal provision lets each side name an appraiser, with an umpire to decide what the appraisers cannot resolve. Mr. Bingham addresses two questions: whether appraisal is the appropriate remedy for the dispute at hand, and whether the appraisal provision was used as the policy intends: invoked for a disagreement over the amount of loss rather than coverage, at the right point in the claim, and carried through by appraisers and an umpire acting impartially.

Catastrophe claims also produce very large records: inspection reports, estimates, engineering & adjusting files, correspondence, and payment histories. Reading that record accurately is often the largest part of the analysis.

s.h: What happens when an insurer fails.

When an insurer is financially troubled, the state regulator can place it under supervision, rehabilitation, or liquidation. A court-appointed receiver, often the insurance commissioner acting through a special deputy, then takes control of the company with the goal of protecting policyholders and creditors: continuing or transferring coverage where possible, marshaling assets, and resolving claims.

The work of an estate is largely operational. Claims against the estate must be evaluated and adjudicated; reserves must be tested; reinsurance must be billed and collected; and the state guaranty associations, which pay many covered claims of insolvent insurers, must be coordinated with. Receivers also pursue claims against former directors, officers, and professionals.

Policyholders, beneficiaries, and producers are affected too. They may contest a rehabilitation plan, or need to understand what happens to their coverage and benefits, a question that is especially pressing when a life or annuity carrier fails.

As a reinsurance expert witness, Mr. Bingham draws on years of practice in the field, on the carrier and regulatory sides, in disputes between ceding insurers and their reinsurers.
How reinsurance disputes arise.

Reinsurance is insurance for insurers. A ceding insurer (the cedent) transfers part of its risk to one or more reinsurers, either one policy at a time under facultative certificates or across a whole book of business under treaties. The relationship frequently depends on the cedent’s reporting: timely notice of claims, accurate reserves, and cooperation with the reinsurer’s rights to inspect records and to participate in significant claims.

Disputes arise over late notice, the cedent’s reserving & claim handling, the allocation & aggregation of losses, the reinsurer’s obligation to follow the cedent’s settlements, and the collection of balances due. Many are resolved by arbitration under the contract’s terms; others reach court, including suits to collect what is owed after an arbitration award. Reinsurance recoverables are also among the most important assets of an insurer in receivership or run-off.

Long-tail claims that surface decades after the policies were written and run through many years and layers of coverage. Mr. Bingham has worked these claims from a carrier’s home office, from inside the industry’s asbestos settlement facility, and as a testifying expert.
How these claims differ.

Asbestos, environmental, and mass tort claims are long-tail exposures. The injury or contamination often comes to light years or decades after the policies were issued, so a single claim can reach many policy periods, several carriers, and both primary and excess layers, and then pass on to those carriers’ reinsurers.

Disputes turn on which policies are triggered, how losses are allocated across years and layers, how defense and remediation costs are apportioned, whether reserves were adequate, and whether notice was timely, including notice to reinsurers. Because these books are large and run for decades, how a carrier organizes, reserves, and documents them is often the question in the case.

b: Reserve adequacy studies.
Whether the reserves an insurer holds match what its claim files support, case by case and in total.

s.h: Testing what is held against what is supported by the documentation in the file.
b: Testing what is held against what is supported by the documentation in the file.

A case reserve is an insurer’s estimate of what it will ultimately pay on an individual claim; bulk and IBNR reserves cover claims not yet reported or not yet fully developed. Together they are the largest liability on most property and casualty balance sheets, and understating them can hide an insolvency until it is too late to prevent.

A reserve adequacy study reviews the claim files behind the reserves: the facts of each claim, the exposure, the handling to date, and the likely outcome. It then compares what is held with what the files support and reports the shortfall or redundancy for the book as a whole. Regulators, receivers, reinsurers, acquirers, and the company’s own management all rely on the result.

Testimony in insurer insolvency.

When an insurer becomes insolvent, the state insurance regulator typically asks a court to place it in rehabilitation or liquidation, and a receiver takes control of the company. The receiver’s task is to marshal the company’s assets, resolve claims against the estate and, where the failure was caused by misconduct or negligence, pursue those responsible.

b: What an insurance expert witness does.

An insurance expert witness explains to a court, a jury, or an arbitration panel how insurance actually works: how policies are written and administered, how claims are investigated, evaluated, reserved, and paid, and what the industry treats as reasonable practice. The expert’s opinions are usually set out first in a written report, then tested in deposition and, if the case goes forward, at trial.

Insurance experts are called in a wide range of disputes: bad-faith and breach-of-contract suits between policyholders and insurers, coverage disputes, reinsurance litigation & arbitration, professional-liability claims against claims administrators, agents, and defense counsel, and receivership proceedings brought on behalf of state regulators. They may be retained by either side, and in insolvency matters by the court-appointed receiver of a failed insurer.

In federal court and in many states, expert testimony must rest on sufficient facts and a reliable method, reliably applied to the facts of the case. That is why the record matters: an opinion is only as strong as its connection to the claim file, the policy, and the standard that applied at the time.

b: When the claims professional is the defendant.

Third-party administrators handle claims on behalf of insurers, self-insured employers, public entities, and risk pools, under a claim service agreement that sets out their authority, service standards, and reporting duties. When results disappoint, the client may sue the TPA for breach of that agreement or for negligence, alleging late investigation, incorrect coverage decisions, inadequate reserves, or poor documentation.

Similar claims are brought against other claims professionals: insurance agencies accused of errors and omissions or of violating the state insurance code, and defense counsel accused by an insurer or excess carrier of mishandling a defense or failing to give timely notice. These cases are usually decided file by file, measured against the agreement, the applicable regulations, and customary industry practice, and often on tight defense timelines.

b: Reserve studies for carriers.
Reserve adequacy work where solvency is in question.
Reserves and solvency.

An insurer’s solvency depends on the adequacy of its reserves. When a carrier is under regulatory scrutiny, in supervision, or in receivership, the question of what its claims will really cost decides whether it can be rehabilitated, must be liquidated, or has been misstating its condition.

Reserve studies in this setting are often contested: they may be presented in court, relied on by a regulator deciding whether to act, or used in litigation over how the company reached its condition.
